paragraphs: First ask whether you are willing to continually assess patient function, medical risks, and rehabilitation goals, then clearly document examination evidence, treatment plans, team responsibilities, and reassessment results. This is a physician position: diagnosis, prescribing, and treatment procedures must remain within your own practice registration, competence, and institutional authorization. Beginners may observe public processes or complete written exercises with entirely fictional cases, without accessing real patient information or replacing clinical decisions. If you enjoy exercise guidance alone, independently compare the training and licensing requirements of therapist occupations.

Signs of fit include connecting functional assessment, patient goals, treatment team handovers, and reassessment records into an explainable chain and actively checking uncertain results. Next, check official local qualification requirements, interview qualified practitioners, observe institution-permitted workflows, and assess training duration and personal commitment. If unwilling to assume continuing medical responsibility, compare adjacent occupations first; personality or interest tests cannot replace these specific checks.

Safe trial (entirely fictional, written organization only): the materials describe a fictional adult reporting reduced walking endurance after an outpatient referral, with medical history, examination results, and contraindication information all marked 'pending verification.' List functional goals and risk questions for a qualified physician to investigate, diagram communication among the physician, therapist, and patient, and state which judgments cannot be reached because information is insufficient. Deliver a one-page question list, a one-page collaboration process, and a one-page uncertainty record; do not assess, prescribe for, or treat real patients.
Written exercises cannot establish clinical competence; real diagnosis and treatment must be the responsibility of qualified, institution-authorized physicians.

If willing to undertake long-term functional assessment, medical risk judgment, interdisciplinary coordination, follow-up reassessment, and physician responsibility, next check local physician registration, rehabilitation medicine training, and actual position requirements. Contact formal education or training institutions to confirm duration and costs, then interview practicing physicians about outpatient clinics, wards, and on-call arrangements. If your main interest is exercise training, compare the independent qualifications and duties of adjacent occupations such as physical therapists; collaborative tasks do not make licenses directly interchangeable.

Face-to-face communication | 84% of respondents have face-to-face discussions daily; patient goals require communication.
Close contact | In the O*NET work context survey, 80% selected the physical proximity category 'very close (near touching).' Functional examinations and rehabilitation assessments may involve contact, but specific procedures, infection prevention, accompanying-person arrangements, and whether remote methods are appropriate depend on patient circumstances and institutional rules; this percentage is not a fixed contact frequency for all positions.
Controlled indoor environment | In the O*NET survey, 88% reported working in a controlled indoor environment daily. Outpatient rooms, wards, and treatment areas may all fall into this category; specific scheduling and off-site duties depend on institutional positions. Environment percentages alone cannot establish workload or infection risk.
Clinical decision freedom | In the O*NET survey, 88% reported considerable decision freedom, reflecting the professional judgment needed for physician assessment, planning, and referral. Discretion remains constrained by practice registration scope, clinical evidence, patient wishes, institutional authorization, and teamwork; it does not permit working beyond competence or omitting review.
Team contact | In the O*NET survey, 60% reported constant contact with others; rehabilitation physicians often connect patients, families, therapists, and other physicians. Constant contact percentages do not establish consultation duration or replace actual scheduling and staffing information.
Task and goal prioritization | In the O*NET survey, 56% reported considerable freedom to determine tasks and priorities. Physicians may order assessments, records, and reassessments, but acute changes, warning signs, or referral needs require prioritizing patient risk and institutional procedures; autonomy does not mean handovers are unnecessary.
Weekly working hours | In the O*NET work context survey, 75% reported a typical workweek exceeding 40 hours. This describes US respondents' work-hour categories, not uniform Chinese rehabilitation physician hours or a guarantee of on-call duties. When seeking work, check written contracts, schedules, on-call compensation, and ward coverage requirements.
Assessment and record accuracy | In the O*NET survey, 56% considered high accuracy extremely important. Errors in functional examinations, medical records, and treatment goals may affect subsequent medical plans, so check scale methods, key medical histories, and handover information. Survey percentages are not medical error rates; specific quality control follows institutional rules.
Telephone and referral communication | In the O*NET survey, 64% reported telephone conversations daily. Calls may connect patients, teams, or referral institutions, but clinical decisions and important handovers still require documentation under institutional rules. This percentage does not establish an individual's daily call count or replace actual local communication channels.

entries.answer: Daily tasks vary by outpatient or inpatient setting and patient conditions. Rehabilitation physicians first check histories, warning signs, examination findings, and patient goals, then assess strength, mobility, sensation, communication, or other functional problems. They form medical diagnoses and rehabilitation goals, document treatment plans, and divide duties with physical therapists, occupational therapists, and other physicians. Subsequent work involves observing treatment responses, repeating functional measurements, and adjusting plans. Specific procedures and signing responsibilities must comply with individual physician registration scope, competence, and institutional authorization; team work cannot all be assigned to a single role.
entries.question: What do physical medicine and rehabilitation physicians do each day?

entries.answer: They collaborate in the same rehabilitation team but have different training paths, qualifications, and final responsibilities. Rehabilitation physicians assess disease and medical risks within physician scope, assume medical diagnosis, medical decision, and treatment plan responsibility, and decide on referral or escalation. Physical and occupational therapists provide functional training, mobility or daily activity interventions, and outcome records under their own professional qualifications. Specific duties follow jurisdictional and institutional rules. O*NET lists these as separate occupations; teamwork or similar skills do not mean license recognition, and therapist qualifications do not directly permit physician practice.
entries.question: How do rehabilitation physicians differ from therapists?

entries.answer: Check qualification thresholds separately from work interests. To become a physician, check local medical education, physician qualifications, practice registration, clinical training, and actual rehabilitation medicine position requirements; short courses or interest tests cannot replace these steps. Then use public position descriptions, compliant placements, or practitioner discussions to observe willingness to handle uncertain conditions, functional assessment, team communication, and reassessment records over the long term. Use entirely fictional cases to list known facts, information to investigate, warning signs, and referral conditions for qualified feedback. Exercises inform learning interests and thinking styles, not clinical competence or practice qualifications; also check formal paths and costs with local medical schools or training institutions.

entries.answer: There are currently no verifiable rehabilitation medicine physician AI replacement rates, adoption rates, or net employment impacts. Literature searches and draft records may see early tool trials, while actual functional assessment, diagnosis, treatment planning, patient communication, and medical record signing still involve clinical evidence, privacy, institutional authorization, and physician responsibility. Judge job effects by how specific institutions validate, purchase, and organize work rather than draw conclusions directly from model demonstrations.

description.text: Physical medicine and rehabilitation physicians assess patients' functional abilities and rehabilitation needs, diagnose and treat related diseases or injuries, and develop and monitor rehabilitation plans. Tasks listed by O*NET include examining mobility, strength, communication, or cognition; documenting examination findings, treatment plans, and outcomes; and coordinating with physical therapists, occupational therapists, and other team members. Specific diagnosis and treatment must comply with the physician's registered practice scope and institutional authorization in the jurisdiction of practice.
